analysis.investment_thesis: Inox Wind is a capital-intensive, policy-dependent wind turbine manufacturer that spent six straight years (2018–2023) destroying capital with negative earnings and catastrophic free cash flows. A single year of profitability in FY25 does not erase a decade of poor returns on a commoditised product in a cyclical industry dependent on government tenders.
key_strengths: Revenue recovered sharply to INR 3,557 Cr in FY25 — near the 2016 peak — suggesting the wind sector policy cycle has turned favorably
Debt is being reduced: borrowings fell from INR 2,637 Cr (2022) to INR 1,140 Cr (2025), improving the balance sheet after the equity raise
Forward P/E of 15.8x is materially lower than trailing 33.7x, implying the market expects earnings to continue recovering
key_risks: Free cash flow has been negative every year since 2021 (FY25: -INR 483 Cr) — the business is still consuming cash despite reported profits due to heavy capex of INR 620 Cr
No durable competitive advantage: wind turbine components are commoditised and subject to intense price competition from Suzlon, Siemens Gamesa, and Chinese OEMs
Returns are structurally mediocre: ROE 11.7%, ROCE 11.5% even in a good year, well below my 15% threshold — this is a business that barely earns its cost of capital
red_flags: Nine-year revenue CAGR of -2.4% — the company is not actually a growth business; it is a cyclical that fluctuates with policy
Six consecutive years of net losses (2018–2023) wiped out equity and required emergency fundraising — management failed catastrophically during the last down-cycle
OCF positive only 1 of the last 5 years, and cumulative FCF over the period is deeply negative — the reported net profit does not translate to cash
analysis.detailed_analysis:
I look for businesses that generate high returns on capital consistently, not businesses that alternate between feast and famine based on government procurement cycles. Inox Wind's history is precisely that: INR 461 Cr profit in 2016, then six years of losses totalling over INR 2,000 Cr, then a recovery in FY25. This is not a wonderful business — it is a cyclical capital-intensive manufacturer with no pricing power operating in an industry where the customer (government utilities) holds all the negotiating leverage.

Even in the best year (FY25), FCF remains negative at -INR 483 Cr because the business needs massive ongoing capital investment to fulfil orders. ROE of 11.7% in a boom year is telling — when the cycle turns again, equity will be destroyed. At 33.7x trailing P/E for a company with this history, I see no margin of safety. I would not own this business at any price that reflects a normalised cycle.
